newsitem.title: USA: US August jobs offers worrisome inflation signals.
newsitem.headline: US August jobs offers worrisome inflation signals.

text.p: A sharp drop in the unemployment rate and ample gains in the earnings portion of the U.S. August payrolls report sends worrisome inflation signals to Federal Reserve policymakers, economists said on Friday.

"This is really going to get the inflation hawks squawking," said Matthew Alexy, chief market strategist at CS First Boston. "The wages are running at levels that I think should be considered troublesome ... I think the Fed is going to have to think seriously about inflation."

On Friday, the U.S. Labor Department reported a rise of 250,000 in August non-farm payrolls versus a revised 228,000 advance in July. Economists surveyed by Reuters had been calling for a gain of 244,000 non-farm jobs.

The average hourly earnings component of the report -- a key gauge of inflation pressures -- posted a heady 0.5 percent rise to $11.87 per hour versus $11.81 in July, while the unemployment rate slid to 5.1 percent, the lowest level since March of 1989.
Economists had expected earnings to rise at a 0.3 percent pace and the jobless rate to fall to 5.3 from 5.4 percent.

Wage inflation worries have featured prominently in recent speeches from Fed officials, and the August hourly earnings figures would appear to lend additional credence to these concerns, economists said.
"The hourly earnings are up big that's got to bother some folks at the Fed," said Joseph Liro, chief economist at CIBC-Wood Gundy Securities Corp.
Liro predicted the Fed would "address" these concerns at its upcoming Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting on September 24.
In contrast to the worrisome inflation signals in the report were encouraging signs that growth may be under control.
"It's the inflation side which is a worry but on the growth side you're okay," said Alexy. "You can make an argument for slowing economic momentum looking at private sector job creation."

Of the 250,000 non-farm jobs created in August, a proportionally heady 77,000 were in the government sector. And the drop in the unemployment rate was partially attributable to a contraction in the labor force of nearly 300,000.

Katherine Abraham, Commissioner of the Bureau of Labor Statistics said some of this drop -- and the consequent jobless rate fall -- could be explained by the late timing of the survey reference week in August.
She said the survey week may have captured more of the normal seasonal movement out of the labor force at the end of the summer.
However, "at least some of the improvement in the unemployment rate is unrelated to the timing of the survey reference period," she cautioned.
Regardless of quirks that may have distorted certain aspects of the August report, economists were clearly worried about the wage figures.

"This pushes deep into the inflation threshold," said Dan Seto, senior economist at Nikko Securities Co International Inc. "I think a 25-basis point hike is very likely now (at the September 24 FOMC meeting)."
Consumer price and retail sales data for August, due in one week, now take on added importance for the Fed and the markets, economists said.
After an initial plunge, the bond market seized on the encouraging growth aspects of the jobs report and rose into positive territory.
At 0945 EDT/1345 GMT the benchmark 6.75 percent 30-year bond was up 2/32 at 95-03/32 to yield 7.15 percent, while the 6.125 percent two-year note was unchanged at 99-16/32 to yield 6.40 percent.
